How to use the simulator

1 Quick start · 2 Top bar · 3 Tabs · 4 DCS console · 5 Faceplates · 6 Trends and alarms · 7 SIS · 8 Field · 9 Exercises · 10 Debrief and data export · 11 Symbols and colours

1 · Quick start

  1. Click anywhere once so the browser allows alarm sound. Check the top bar shows 🔔 Sound on.
  2. The session opens at design: 60 m³/h of light hydrocarbon feed from surge drum V-201 is split in depropanizer C-201 into propane overhead (about 32 m³/h) and butane-and-heavier bottoms (about 28 m³/h) at 1.70 MPa g. Open P&ID to see the plant, then DCS console to operate it.
  3. Go to Exercises, pick a list (Training, Think EQUIPPED or Procedures) and click Load. A blue banner gives the situation; click Acknowledge on the banner to hide it.
  4. Operate from the DCS console: click an instrument bubble, a valve or a pump to open its faceplate on the right. Hand valves, pump auto-start switches, the telephone to the upstream unit and outside checks are on the Field tab.
  5. Use Speed to run faster (2×–50×) and Freeze to pause while you think. Compositions and levels move over tens of minutes: use 10× or 20×.
  6. When finished, open Debrief and grading for your score, then Data export to download CSV files for your report.

2 · Top bar

ControlWhat it does
ClockSimulated time since the session or exercise started (hh:mm:ss). Cases that begin part-way through a problem show the earlier history with negative times (−00:30:00).
Freeze / RunPauses and resumes the simulation. Nothing changes while frozen, but you can still read and click.
Speed1× to 50× real time. Grading uses simulated time, so speed does not change your score.
Status lampGreen: heating on, with the feed-drum configuration (rev A, B or C). Amber: heating off. Red: SIS tripped or PSV-201 relieving. Click it to open the SIS screen.
🔔 Sound on / 🔕 Sound offOne short beep = new alarm; two alternating tones = trip or relief. It repeats until acknowledged or silenced.
SilenceStops the sound only. Alarms keep flashing until acknowledged. A new alarm sounds again.
AcknowledgeAcknowledges every alarm in the list. Unacknowledged alarms older than 60 s cost points.
ScoreContinuous score for this session (starts at 100).

3 · Tabs

The tabs are arranged in six groups (top row); the second row shows the tabs of the chosen group, and each group remembers the tab you last opened. P&ID sits under both Process & Design and Operate, Safety layers under both Process & Design and Safety, and SOP under both Operability and Train & Assess: it is the same page in each place. On a phone the second row becomes a drop-down list.

4 · DCS console

  • Overview: all main loops and a summary at top left (feed, column, top product, bottoms, margin).
  • Column profile: tray temperatures from tray 1 to tray 27 drawn beside the column (dashed = design), flood indices, product qualities. A profile that moves up or down the column tells you more than any single temperature.
  • Overhead: pressure (PIC-210 and the independent PI-211), vent to fuel gas, PSV-201, cooling water and condenser duty, reflux ratio, reflux pumps.
  • Bottoms and reboiler: LP header, XV-209, TV-208, steam flow and steam chest pressure, reboiler duty, sump level, bottoms and their quality.
  • Feed system: V-201, feed pumps, FV-201, preheater E-201 and the vapour fraction of the feed. As built (rev A) the V-201 level and the upstream rate are not on the DCS.
  • Profitability: dollars per hour and totals for feed, products, steam, cooling water, vent and flare, with the product specifications. Off-spec product is sold at a lower price.

Instrument bubbles follow ISA style: letters on top, loop number below, live value next to it, controller mode (MAN, AUTO, CAS) at upper right. A red value is in alarm; a flashing value is not yet acknowledged. A square around a bubble marks a trip or auto-start switch (FSLL, LSLL, LSHH).

5 · Faceplates

PartWhat it does
PV, barsLarge number is the measured value. The PV bar shows it on the range; the tick shows the set point; the OUT bar shows the valve signal.
Manual / Automatic / CascadeManual: you set OUT. Automatic: you set SP. Cascade: FIC-204 takes its set point from TIC-227; FIC-201 takes it from LIC-201 (rev C only). While the secondary is not in Cascade the primary output tracks the secondary set point so the switch is bumpless.
SP and OUT fields, − / +Type a value and press Enter, or step it. SP is locked in Cascade; OUT works only in Manual.
TuningGain, reset (s) and rate (s). Changes take effect on Apply and are logged.
Pumps and hand valvesClick a pump or HV-2xx on the drawing. A tripped pump will not restart until the fault is cleared; a gas-bound pump runs but pumps nothing until it is primed.

6 · Trend and alarm summary

  • Trend group: Column, Feed system, Overhead, Bottoms and reboiler, Product quality, or Selected tag (PV, SP and OUT of the open faceplate). Window 5–60 min; each pen has its own range in the legend.
  • Alarm summary: newest unacknowledged first. Click a row to acknowledge it and open that instrument.

7 · Safety system (SIS)

Button / panelWhat it does
Reset SISClears a trip and reopens XV-201. Refused while a high-level cause is still present.
Enable heatingOpens XV-209 (reboiler) and XV-202 (preheater) when every start permissive is green: SIS reset, cooling water ≥ 250 m³/h, sump ≥ 30 %, TIC-208 and TIC-202 in MAN at ≤ 10 %, steam blocks open.
Stop heating (normal)Planned isolation of both steam supplies; not counted as a trip.
Emergency shutdownImmediate trip: XV-201, XV-209 and XV-202 close, TIC-208, TIC-202 and FIC-201 go to MAN at 0 %.
Trip conditionsAmber ● = present now; ▶ in red = first-out cause of the last trip.
Feed-drum upgradesRev B puts the V-201 level on the DCS with low and high alarms, and a low-flow alarm on FIC-201. Rev C adds LIC-201, cascaded onto FIC-201, so the drum level sets the feed.

8 · Field

  • Pumps P-201A (motor) / P-201B (steam turbine) and P-202A/B, with the auto-start switches HS-201B and HS-202B. An auto-start disarms itself after it acts.
  • Block valves: HV-216 cooling water, HV-209 reboiler steam, HV-202 preheater steam, HV-210 vent to fuel gas.
  • LG-201: the only level indication of V-201 in rev A, with the outside operator's rounds log.
  • Feed pumps: look and listen, and prime a gas-bound pump (1 minute; it only works with liquid above the suction).
  • Telephone to the upstream unit: ask what they send (answer after 2 minutes) or ask for a new rate.
  • Flare and PSV-201, and local gauges (PG, TG, LG) that are independent of the DCS transmitters.

9 · Exercises

  • Load an exercise: the plant is reset to its starting state; faults appear on their own schedule. Some troubleshooting cases start part-way through a problem that began before you arrived; the trends and the event log show that history with negative times.
  • Procedure tracker: steps tick with their time when the simulator sees them done (! = done out of order). Tick Communicated and press Finish and grade (it also grades itself at the time limit).
  • What-if, Trend matching, Scrambles, DCS reading sheet: as labelled; each result goes to the Debrief tab.

10 · Debrief and data export

  • Debrief: score with each deduction, performance, exercise grades, fault recovery times and the event log (filter and copy).
  • Data export: tick the data sets, choose range and interval, then download. The column profile file lists every tray (pressure, temperature, composition, holdup) against design. Files are UTF-8 CSV with # header lines. Nothing is kept after you close the page.

Trainee workbook · Depropanizer Column Ver 1

Work through Parts A to G in order. Record your answers and evidence (screenshots, CSV files) as you go; your report is built from them.

1 Purpose · 2 The unit · 3 Control scheme · 4 Safety systems · 5 Operating rules · 6 Activities A–G · 7 Grading · 8 Report checklist

1 · Purpose

This workbook trains you to operate, monitor and troubleshoot a depropanizer: a 27-tray distillation column that takes propane and everything lighter overhead and sends butane and heavier to a debutanizer. By the end you should be able to:

  1. Read the P&ID and the DCS displays and state the normal value and alarm limits of every key tag.
  2. Explain how pressure, boilup, reflux, feed rate, feed composition and feed vaporization move the tray temperature profile and the product qualities, and predict the direction every key variable moves after a disturbance.
  3. Start up the column safely from cold: fill, heat, vent the start-up gas, total reflux, pressurize, feed and products.
  4. Keep every inventory in the unit under control, including the ones nobody instrumented.
  5. Recognise an abnormal situation from alarms, trends and field checks, keep the unit safe, and find the root cause with a systematic six-stage method.
  6. Propose a permanent improvement and support it with exported data.

2 · The unit

Liquid feed from an upstream unit collects in horizontal surge drum V-201 (2 m × 7.9 m) at −1 °C, at its bubble point. V-201 has no level controller: as built (rev A) only a local gauge glass, LG-201, shows its level. Feed pump P-201A (motor; P-201B steam turbine is the spare, auto-started by FSLL-201) sends the feed through FV-201 (FIC-201) and preheater E-201, where LP steam under TIC-202 heats it to 75 °C and vaporizes about two thirds of it, to tray 18 of C-201. The trays are numbered from the bottom. Overhead vapour is condensed in E-202 with cooling water that is not controlled; the liquid collects in reflux drum V-202. Non-condensable gas (methane, hydrogen) collects in the condenser and is vented to fuel gas through PV-210, and that vent sets the column pressure (PIC-210): venting gas uncovers condenser surface, more vapour condenses, the pressure falls. PSV-201 relieves to flare at 1.80 MPa g. Reflux pumps P-202A/B return reflux under FIC-204 (TIC-227 can cascade onto it) and send propane to storage under LIC-203. Thermosyphon reboiler E-203 boils up under TIC-208 on tray 8 (TV-208); the bottoms flow to the debutanizer on pressure alone under LIC-202.

Values are the model's design point with noise off. The case gives temperatures and pressures but no flow rates: the flows, compositions, drum levels, cooling water and steam conditions are engineering assumptions chosen to be consistent with a 2 m depropanizer at 1.70 MPa g, a 75 °C feed 67 % vaporized, a 45 °C top and a 109 °C bottom. The components are lumped as "C3 and lighter" and "C4 and heavier".

3 · Control scheme

LoopMeasuresMovesValve on air failureNotes
FIC-201Feed flow FT-201FV-201Fail closedDraws its set point whatever V-201 holds (rev A). Rev C: set point from LIC-201.
TIC-202Feed after E-201TV-202 LP steamFail closedSets the feed vaporization.
PIC-210Column top pressurePV-210 vent to fuel gasFail openDirect acting: high pressure opens the vent. Slow: it works through the gas inventory of the condenser.
FIC-204Reflux flowFV-204Fail openNormally AUTO with a fixed set point; Cascade from TIC-227 is available.
TIC-227Tray 27 temperatureRemote set point of FIC-204—Normally MAN (tracking). The top tray is nearly pure propane: its temperature follows the pressure more than the composition.
TIC-208Tray 8 temperatureTV-208 reboiler steamFail closedTray 8 sits where the profile is steep, so it is sensitive to composition.
LIC-202Sump levelLV-202 bottomsFail closedBottoms leave on the pressure difference (1.72 → 0.48 MPa g).
LIC-203Reflux drum levelLV-203 propane productFail closed
HV-216, HV-209, HV-202, HV-210—Field block valves—Cooling water, reboiler steam, preheater steam, vent. Operated from the Field tab.

Two integrators in series. V-201 holds the running difference between what the upstream unit sends and what FIC-201 draws; the C-201 sump holds the difference between the liquid from tray 1 and the bottoms plus the boilup. The sump has a controller; in rev A the drum does not. Either the drum level sets the feed (the column follows upstream) or the feed is fixed (the drum absorbs the difference and somebody must watch it).

4 · Safety systems

SIS: reboiler steam (XV-209) and preheater steam (XV-202) open only from IDLE with every start permissive met. A trip closes them, puts TIC-208 and TIC-202 in MAN at 0 % and latches the first-out cause; a high-level trip or ESD also closes the feed shut-off XV-201.

Alarm limits

5 · Operating rules

  1. Cooling before heat. Establish cooling water before you heat the reboiler; on loss of cooling water, stop the heat first.
  2. Every inventory needs an owner. A level with no controller must be watched and its inflow and outflow matched by hand: call upstream, read LG-201 every round.
  3. Never above 1.80 MPa g. That is the PSV-201 set point. Normal operation is 1.70; a set point at 1.80 puts the column on its relief valve.
  4. Heat slowly, reflux early. On start-up, return reflux as soon as the reflux drum has liquid; do not draw product before the column is on temperature control.
  5. A running pump is not a pumping pump. Check the discharge pressure and listen. A gas-bound pump must be stopped or primed; running it dry destroys the seal.
  6. Two instruments before you believe one: PIC-210 vs PI-211 and PG-211; TIC-208 vs the tray profile; FIC-201 vs the valve position and the pump.
  7. When something happens right after a change, it may still not be the cause. Write down the time line; ask what else was changing.
  8. Acknowledge every alarm and say out loud what it means.

6 · Activities

Part A · Familiarisation (about 20 min)

  1. Open the P&ID. Trace the feed, overhead, reflux, product, bottoms, steam and vent paths and list every instrument and valve on each.
  2. Visit the six DCS displays. Sketch the tray temperature profile and mark where it is steep.
  3. Complete the DCS reading sheet (Exercises tab). Graded out of 15.
  4. Do a round on the Field tab: LG-201, pumps, flare, local gauges. Download a column profile CSV.

Part B · What-if predictions (about 20 min)

For each event predict ↑ / ↓ / = for all eight variables 30 minutes after the event before pressing Check my predictions. Explain every wrong prediction with a material balance, the relative volatility, or the profile.

Part C · Cold startup (graded, limit 3 h 30 min simulated)

Load Cold startup through the SIS from Procedures. The tracker ticks steps as you complete them:

    Part D · Training exercises

    For each exercise record: first alarm and time, the first variable you noticed, what you did, and the recovery time in Debrief.

    Part E · Think EQUIPPED troubleshooting

    Each case gives only a situation. Work through the six stages and write your evidence for each:

    StageWhat you must produce
    1 EngageIs it dangerous or time-critical? Decide: keep running, safe-park (total reflux) or shut down, and state what would change your mind.
    2 DefineProblem statement (what, where, when, how much, what did not change), IS / IS NOT table, the time line, and a measurable target.
    3 ExploreFundamentals: every inventory is inflow minus outflow; a tray temperature is a composition at a pressure; pressure is set by vapour made against vapour condensed and vented. Close the balances, compare instruments, list recent changes.
    4 PlanAt least three working hypotheses written so they can fail, each with a test (tag, field check, phone call, what result kills it), ordered by safety, time and cost.
    5 Do itRun the tests, record results, name the root cause, apply the fix; predict the response before each move.
    6 Look backCompare prediction with result, and propose a change that stops it happening again (you may test rev B or rev C on the SIS tab).

    Part F · Trend matching and scrambles

    Match four unlabelled trend sets to their events and justify each from the six pens. Put the scramble steps in order.

    Part G · Data and report

    For your Part C run and TE-1, download the run data (all data sets, 10 s), the column profile and the event log. Plot FIC-201, PIC-210, TIC-208, LIC-202 and the V-201 level against time, and the tray profile before and after your fix.

    7 · How you are graded

    The continuous score starts at 100 and loses points (during start-up, shutdown and emergency procedures the quality and level deductions are paused):

    DeductionRate
    A product off specification while the column runs (C4+ in propane above 2.5 mol %, C3 in bottoms above 2.0 mol %)0.3–2 points/min per product, growing with the error
    PSV-201 passing to flare1 point/min
    Sump or reflux drum below 10–15 % or above 90 %0.5 points/min
    Alarm left unacknowledged over 60 s0.3 points/min per alarm
    Unplanned SIS trip caused by operation (trips that follow an equipment failure are not charged)15 points each
    Feed pump left running gas-bound for 5 minutes (seal damage)10 points each

    Procedures, the reading sheet, what-if, trend matching and scrambles are graded separately under Exercise grades in the Debrief tab. The Profitability display shows the money each decision makes or loses.

    8 · Report checklist

    • Part A sketches, reading-sheet score and column profile CSV.
    • Part B predictions with corrections.
    • Part C procedure grade, time to line out, and trend plots.
    • Part D table for every exercise.
    • Part E six-stage worksheet for each assigned case, with evidence (trends, balances, field checks, phone calls).
    • Debrief screenshot: score, deductions and exercise grades.
    • One recommended improvement, with before/after data.

    2 · What the alternative version adds to the PFD

    • Every valve: suction and discharge block valves and check valves on both pump pairs (MV-201 to MV-204, NRV-201/202; MV-211 to MV-214, NRV-211/212), the block-and-bypass set around FV-201 (MV-205, MV-206, MV-207), the steam block valves HV-202 and HV-209, the vent block HV-210 and the cooling-water block HV-216.
    • Every instrument with its ISA-5.1 bubble: plain circle = field transmitter or switch, circle with a bar = DCS console, circle in a square = SIS. Field transmitters are drawn apart from their functions (FT-201, TT-208, LT-202, LT-203, PT-210, PT-211, FT-204, PDT-230).
    • Safety devices: PSV-201 on the overhead line to flare, the SIS shut-off valves XV-201 (feed), XV-202 (preheater steam) and XV-209 (reboiler steam), level switches LS-202 and LS-203 on their own nozzles.
    • Utilities: LP steam to E-201 and E-203 with flow elements and steam traps ST-201 / ST-202, cooling water to E-202 with FE-216, TI-214 and TI-215.
    • Line numbers (size – service – number), drains and vents, the design case in note 1 and the interlock schedule on the sheet.

    LoopMeasuresMovesValve failsWhy that fail position

    4 · Interlock schedule (SIS)

    TagCauseSettingDelayAction
    LSLL-202C-201 sump low-low (armed only with the SIS in RUN)< 5 %5 sTrip: heat off
    LSHH-203V-202 reflux drum high-high (liquid to fuel gas)> 92 %5 sTrip: heat and feed off

    Every trip closes XV-209 (reboiler steam) and XV-202 (preheater steam) and puts TIC-208 and TIC-202 in MAN at 0 %. LSHH-203 and the ESD also close XV-201 and put FIC-201 in MAN at 0 %, so the feed stops. Reset is blocked while a cause is present. Heating is re-opened only when FI-216 ≥ 250 m³/h, LIC-202 ≥ 30 %, TIC-208 and TIC-202 are in MAN at ≤ 10 %, and HV-209 and HV-202 are open.

    5 · Differences from rev C (the reference drawing above)

    • Pumps drawn with their suction and discharge block valves and check valves (the screen shows the drives only: motor for P-201A and P-202A/B, steam turbine for P-201B).
    • The interlock marks I-1 (LSHH-203) and I-2 (LSLL-202) become rows of an interlock schedule, together with the FSLL-201 and PDSL-230 auto-starts and PSV-201.
    • Field transmitters shown separately from the DCS and SIS functions, so shared-sensor questions are visible: LT-202 and LS-202, LT-203 and LS-203, PT-210 and PT-211 each sit on their own nozzle. PDI-230 on the screen is the DCS indication of PDT-230, and PDSL-230 is its auto-start switch.

          1 · What a block flow diagram is

          A block flow diagram (BFD) is the simplest drawing of a process: each operation is a box, each main stream is a line with an arrow, and the streams carry numbers that point to a table. It answers what goes where and how much, before anyone decides what the equipment looks like. For the depropanizer it shows one feed coming in, three products going out (propane, bottoms, vent gas), the internal reflux loop and the three utilities (LP steam twice, cooling water once). The engineering drawings of a unit are read in this order:

          DrawingWhat it showsWhat it leaves outUsed forOn this simulator
          BFDOperations as blocks (feed drum, pumps, preheater, column, condenser, reflux drum, reboiler), main streams 1–11, overall flows and compositionsEquipment shapes, trays, valves, instruments, the column internalsConcept, overall mole, light-key and energy balances, explaining the unit to a new operatorThis tab; section 2 of the Process tab
          PFDEvery major equipment item with its symbol and tag (C-201 with its trays, E-201/202/203, V-201/202, P-201A/B, P-202A/B), the control valves and main loops (FIC-201, TIC-202, FIC-204, TIC-208, LIC-202/203, PIC-210), stream flags with flow, T and PHand valves, drains, bypasses, most local instruments, line sizesProcess design, equipment sizing, heat and material balance, HAZIDPFD tab (DC-PFD-200)
          P&IDEvery line, block valve (HV-202, HV-209, HV-210, HV-216), instrument loop, fail position, the SIS valves XV-201/202/209, trip switches (LSLL-202, LSHH-203, FSLL-201, PDSL-230) and PSV-201Flows and conditions (these stay in the data sheets and the stream table)Detailed design, HAZOP, construction, operation and maintenanceP&ID tab; the live copy is the DCS console

          6 · From BFD to PFD

          • Each block becomes one or more equipment items with a tag and a symbol: "C-201" becomes a tray column with the feed tray, the control tray and the sump drawn in; "E-203" becomes a thermosyphon reboiler piped to the sump; "P-201A/B" becomes two pumps in parallel.
          • The control valves appear on the lines they throttle: FV-201 on the feed, TV-202 and TV-208 on the steam, FV-204 on the reflux, LV-203 on the propane, LV-202 on the bottoms and PV-210 on the vent, each with its controller.
          • Each numbered stream gets a flag with flow, temperature and pressure at design, so the drawing carries its own heat and material balance (the table in section 4).
          • The P&ID then adds every block valve, drain, vent, instrument loop, the SIS valves and trips, and PSV-201. See the PFD and P&ID tabs.

          Process flow diagram (PFD) · DC-PFD-200

          1 What a PFD adds · 2 The drawing · 3 Equipment list · 4 Stream flags and the model · 5 Reading the PFD · 6 From PFD to P&ID

          1 · What a PFD adds to the block flow diagram

          • Equipment symbols and tags (ISO 10628 conventions): the column with its trays, the horizontal feed and reflux drums, the pumps in pairs, the steam preheater, the water-cooled condenser and the thermosyphon reboiler.
          • Control, shut-off and relief valves on the lines they act on: FV-201, TV-202, FV-204, LV-203, TV-208, LV-202 and PV-210; the SIS valves XV-201, XV-202 and XV-209; PSV-201 to the flare.
          • Stream flags: flow, temperature and pressure at the design point on every numbered stream, so the drawing carries its own material balance.
          • Battery limits: the upstream unit, propane storage, the debutanizer, the fuel-gas and flare systems, and the steam and cooling-water utilities.

          A PFD leaves out hand valves, drains, instrument loops, line sizes and most instruments; those belong on the P&ID.

            4 · Stream flags and the model

            The flags on the drawing are the model's design point, rounded (Drawing); Design is the same point unrounded (noise off); the Now columns come from the live plant: when you change a set point or a disturbance develops, the drawing stays at design and the plant moves away from it. Streams that no meter reads show "not metered" here, as on the console.

            #StreamFlow unitFlowT °CP kPa g
            DrawingDesignNowDrawingDesignNowDrawingDesignNow

            5 · Reading the PFD

            • One feed, two products. Follow the feed 1 → 2 → 3 into tray 18; the light part leaves the top as vapour (4), is condensed and split into reflux (5) and propane product (6); the heavy part leaves the sump as bottoms (8). At steady state stream 3 = streams 6 + 8 (+ the small vent 7) on a molar basis.
            • Reflux is internal. Stream 5 goes out and comes straight back: it costs condenser and reboiler duty, not product. The overhead vapour (4) is reflux plus product.
            • Heat in, heat out. Steam enters at E-201 (9) and E-203 (10); cooling water (11) takes the heat out at E-202. The column itself only moves the heat from the reboiler to the condenser while it separates.
            • Pressure sets the temperatures. The top at 1.70 MPa g is chosen so propane condenses against cooling water; every tray temperature follows from the pressure and the composition, which is why tray 8's temperature can stand for the bottoms quality.
            • Pressure falls along each path. Feed: pump discharge (2) → FV-201 → E-201 → tray 18 (3). Liquid products leave on pump pressure (5, 6) or on the column pressure alone (8, into the debutanizer at a lower pressure).

            Operating windows · where C-201 can run, what limits it, and how much room there is

            Teaching slide deck · operability, the variability of feed, cooling water and steam, bounds and the integrity operating window, capacity and turndown, and the Type I, II/III and Monte Carlo windows of the depropanizer, worked on this model.
            Open the deck ↗Same folder (offline / GitHub Pages)

            1 Operability · 2 Variability · 3 Bounds and IOW · 4 Worst case and point check · 5 Capacity and turndown · 6 Type I window · 7 Type II and III window · 8 Monte Carlo window · 9 Holes and limitations

            1 · Operability and the operating window

            Process operability means the plant has the capacity and flexibility to reach a range of operating conditions safely, reliably and profitably, with good dynamic behaviour and on-spec products. The operating window is the range of steady states that can be achieved: every controlled variable at its set point and no limit crossed. Four things shape it.

            The variables of C-201

            ClassVariable (tag)DesignWhy it is in this class

            2 · Variability: the design basis the window must cover

            "The abnormal is normal." A window is only as good as the list of changes it was sized for. The five classes of variability, written as a design-basis memorandum for C-201 (ranges come from the page's alarms and fault library; frequencies and ranges marked "assumed" are teaching values):

            SourceWhat changes on C-201Range used hereHow oftenCovered by

            Seven disturbance variables are treated on this tab: feed rate, feed composition z (C3 and lighter), feed temperature (TI-201 and the TIC-202 preheat set point, which sets the vapour fraction q), cooling-water supply temperature TI-214, LP steam header PI-207, non-condensables in the feed and the downstream pressure of the debutanizer. A single human error must not cause an unsafe condition and must not stay undetected: that is why the bounds in part 3 carry alarms and, where the damage is fast (overpressure, a dry reboiler, liquid to fuel gas), PSV-201 and the SIS trips.

            3 · Bounds and the integrity operating window

            The bounds are the frame of the window. A hard bound cannot be crossed without damage, a release or a trip (relief pressure, sump low-low, reflux drum high-high). A soft bound can be crossed for a while but something degrades (alarm, flaring, a hot top tray). A capacity bound is the end of a handle's travel or of the trays' hydraulic range (flooding, weeping). A CV bound is a product specification. The table reads the running simulator: the limit, the design value, the live value and the margin now as a fraction of the margin at design.

            Bound (OW_B)KindSourceLimitDesignNowMargin now ÷ margin at design

            Reading the IOW. Inside the target band the column holds both products with room on every handle. Between the target and the standard limit it is still safe, but time counts: an alarm is due, a valve near its stop cannot answer the next disturbance, a product drifts toward its spec. Past the critical limit failure is quick: PSV-201 lifts to flare, the trays flood, the SIS trips (Safety layers tab).

            4 · Design for the worst case, and a live point check

            Equipment is sized for the worst case of the variability it must handle, and each piece has its own worst case. The reboiler and the stripping trays see their worst case with a heavy feed at high rate (more bottoms to strip); the condenser, the rectifying trays and the vent see theirs with a light feed at high rate and warm cooling water; the steam valves with a low header; the vent valve at low rate (too little gas to vent) and with many inerts. Pick a case, or set your own point: the page runs one copy of this model to steady state (2 h of plant time, all loops as at design: FIC-201, TIC-202, FIC-204, TIC-208, PIC-210 and both levels in AUTO; trips switched off so limits can be seen) and checks every bound. The live plant is not touched.

            5 · Capacity and turndown

            A column that only just meets the design point is cheap but has no window; a large one has a window but costs capital and wastes energy at low rate. The capacity must be safe, protect the equipment and meet the specs for the base case and frequently occurring variability; lower production is acceptable in rare cases; shut down for extreme ones. Turndown ratio = normal maximum ÷ normal minimum, where "normal" means sustainable without hazard, damage or off-spec product.

            Each element has its own feed range. The column's range is the overlap, so it is always narrower than any single element's. The bars come from a feed sweep in 1 m³/h steps at the design composition, cooling water and header, interpolated between runs. Choose the operating policy: the reflux held at its design set point, or ratioed to the feed.

            ElementTurndown or rangeability on C-201TypicalFlexibility class

            6 · Steady-state operating window, Type I: what the two composition handles can reach

            Write the model as y = A u + B d + C (y controlled variables, u manipulated, d disturbances). Three problems:

            TypeGivenFindOn C-201

            C-201 has two handles on composition: the reflux FIC-204 (how much liquid washes the rising vapour) and the boil-up, set by TIC-208 through TV-208 on the tray-8 temperature. Every cell below is one steady state at design feed, cooling water and header, with the reflux and the tray-8 set point moved from design.

            outlined cells = every bound met · ring = design set points

            7 · Type II and Type III: the disturbances C-201 can absorb

            Now every loop holds its design set point (tray 8 at the TIC-208 set point, reflux, preheat, pressure, levels) while the disturbances move. Type II reads the handle positions each disturbance needs; Type III keeps only the points where every handle is inside its range and every bound holds, and colours the rest by the bound that fails first (hard and capacity bounds before the product specs: root cause before symptom).

            8 · Monte Carlo operating window

            The recipe: (1) simulate the base case, (2) replace the uncertain inputs by samples from their distributions and repeat, (3) mark each sample inside or outside against every bound, (4) report the fraction and show it. Here each sample is interpolated in the Type II grids of part 7 (feed rate × composition × cooling-water temperature, at the design header), and every bound is checked on the interpolated steady state.

            9 · Holes in the window, and what the steady-state window does not tell you

              Flexibility · the handles that steer C-201 through its operating window

              Teaching slide deck · how many handles a column needs, where they act, the reflux–boil-up interaction, flexibility in the pumps, the reboiler and the condenser, production-rate control and composition-control strategies, worked on the depropanizer model.
              Open the deck ↗Same folder (offline / GitHub Pages)

              The Operating windows tab finds where C-201 can run; this tab looks at the handles that move it there. Gains, capacities and responses come from runs on copies of this simulator's model (trips off, the live plant untouched); the curves in parts 5 and 6 are drawn from the model's own equations (pumps, valves, reboiler, condenser), checked against the design state. The pump-speed slider is an illustration: the pumps in the model run at fixed speed.

              1 What flexibility is · 2 How many · 3 Where · 4 Reflux and boil-up · 5 Fluid flow · 6 Heat transfer · 7 Production rate · 8 Control strategies · 9 How much · 10 Recommendations

              1 · What flexibility is

              Flexibility is the ability of a plant to operate reliably across a wide range of rates and conditions without losing quantity or quality. Some controlled variables are held at their set points while disturbances arrive; flexibility is what lets us steer the process after the equipment has been built.

              Without flexibility the column passes every disturbance (a heavier feed, warmer cooling water, a weaker steam header) on to the product purities and the pressure. With flexibility it reaches its set points and compensates the disturbances.

              How it is provided

              • Spare capacity in pumps, valves, reboiler and condenser area, tray hydraulics.
              • Adjustable utility flows: LP steam to E-203 and E-201; the vent that clears non-condensables from E-202.
              • By-passes and recycles: none on C-201 as built (the options are in part 10).

              Four design questions: how many handles, where, which tools (valves, speed, level, by-pass), and how much capacity.

              The flexibility register of C-201

              HandleWhat it adjustsKind of flexibilityAt designSpare at designStatus

              2 · How many handles? Degrees of freedom

              A successful design needs number of adjustable handles ≥ number of variables to be held. The maximum number of controlled variables equals the degrees of freedom; the minimum number of handles equals the number of variables we insist on.

              Variable C-201 must holdWhyHandle used as built

              3 · Where? Causal paths from each handle

              Each held variable needs a handle with an independent causal path to it. Interaction is allowed as long as every desired point can still be reached. Three cases:

              Steady-state effect of a +5 % step on each handle, run on the model (the numbers behind the causal map). Open loop: TIC-208 in manual, so TV-208 stays where it is; every other loop as at design.

              The same steps with TIC-208 in AUTO (as the column is operated). The TV-208 row is replaced by a +1 °C step of the tray-8 set point.

              4 · The classic interaction: reflux and boil-up on both products

              Reflux and boil-up each move both product compositions: more reflux purifies the propane but, at a fixed boil-up, pushes propane down into the bottoms; more boil-up strips the bottoms but carries more C4 up. That is the spring in part 3. Ask for a change in the two analyzers and the page solves the 2 × 2 steady-state model (gains from ±1 % runs on the model, TIC-208 in manual) for the handle moves:

              5 · Flexibility for fluid flow

              For liquids the flow settles where the pump's pressure rise equals the losses: F = √(ΔP / ((fL/D + Kvalve + ΣKj) ρ/2g)). Only the valve term (or the pump speed) is adjustable. C-201 has two pumped systems: the feed from V-201 (0.40 MPa g) up to tray 18 (1.71 MPa g), and the reflux drum outflow split between reflux and product.

              5a · Feed: P-201A with FV-201, or pump speed

              5b · Reflux and product: one pump, two valves (FV-204 and LV-203)

              6 · Flexibility for heat transfer

              Q = U A ΔT: flexibility can act on U (a flow changes a film coefficient; fouling lowers it), on A (area in service: a gas pocket blankets condenser tubes, a low sump level starves a thermosyphon) or on ΔT (the steam's saturation temperature in the chest, the condensing temperature set by the column pressure).

              ExchangerUAΔTHandle as built

              6a · Reboiler E-203: how much spare duty?

              TV-208 does not set the steam flow directly: it sets how much steam can reach the chest, and the chest pressure PI-205 floats until the condensing steam passes the duty through the area, Q = UA (Tsat(PI-205) − Tsump). The curves are the model's own relation for E-203 at the design sump temperature.

              6b · Condenser E-202: cooling water and non-condensables set the pressure

              E-202 has no control valve: the cooling water runs at whatever HV-216 and the pumps give. The pressure is held by the area: non-condensable gas collects in the condenser and blankets part of it; PIC-210 vents gas to fuel gas to uncover area when the pressure rises. The curves show the drum pressure the condenser needs to pass the design duty, from the model relation Q = ε cw (Tc − Tcw), ε = 1 − e−UA(1−a)/cw, with the condensing temperature Tc the bubble point of the overhead.

              7 · Flexibility for production rate

              At steady state material must balance in every vessel and in the whole plant. One flexible variable sets the rate; every other flow follows automatically, and measured flows are never simply matched to each other (meter errors would accumulate in a vessel). Level and pressure show inventory.

              Guiding principleC-201

              The control structure decides how quickly the flexibility is used. From least to most flexible:

              StrategyWhat movesHandles which variabilityOn C-201

              Runs on copies of the model (4 h after the change at t = 10 min). The reflux ratioed to the feed is an illustrative alternative written into the run (FIC-204 set point = design reflux × FI-201 ÷ design feed); the TIC-227 cascade is on the P&ID (MAN at design).

              9 · How much capacity? Spare room on each handle

              Move the feed rate and composition: the bars show how much of each limit is used when the loops hold their design set points (Type II runs of the Operating windows tab, interpolated). The first bar to cross 95 % is the capacity that sets the edge of the window.

              HAZID · Hazard Identification of the depropanizer

              Teaching slide deck · what HAZID is, the PFD and its seven study areas, the guideword checklist for an LPG unit, bow-tie prevention and mitigation, the major accident hazards of a depropanizer and the studies that follow.
              Open the deck ↗Same folder (offline / GitHub Pages)
              1 What HAZID is · 2 Method · 3 PFD and study areas · 4 Guideword checklist · 5 Hazard register · 6 Major accident hazards · 7 From HAZID to HAZOP

              A plant-level, checklist-driven identification of the major hazards around C-201, done before (and wider than) the detailed HAZOP. It uses the same example risk matrix as the HAZOP tab; a real study uses the owner's matrix and a multidisciplinary team.

              1 · What HAZID is and where it sits

              HAZID (Hazard Identification) is a structured brainstorm of what could go badly wrong across the whole facility, including its surroundings, people and environment. It is done early (concept and front-end design) on the PFD, the plot plan and the design basis, so that the major hazards shape the design before the details are fixed. It asks broad questions ("what hazards exist around the reflux drum?"), where HAZOP asks detailed ones ("what if the reflux is more than intended?").

              A depropanizer is an LPG unit: its major hazards come from a large inventory of liquefied gas held above its atmospheric boiling point. A leak flashes to a heavy vapour cloud that drifts along the ground (flash fire, vapour-cloud explosion); a vessel exposed to fire can fail as a BLEVE; the column pressure is set by condensation, so anything that stops the condenser drives the column to its relief valve; and LPG that is depressured cools itself far below the feed temperature (auto-refrigeration). The inventory at the design point of the model:

              HAZIDHAZOP
              WhenConcept / FEED, and before major changesDetailed design, P&ID frozen; revalidation
              DrawingPFD, plot planP&ID, cause-and-effect chart
              BreakdownAreas / systemsNodes with one design intent
              PromptGuideword checklist by hazard category (natural, external, process, utilities, health, occupational, environment, operations)Guide word × parameter (NO flow, MORE pressure, …)
              ScopeProcess and non-process hazards, site and surroundingsProcess deviations and operability
              OutputHazard register, list of major accident hazards, studies to do next (HAZOP, relief and flare, fire and explosion, SIL, layout)Worksheets and recommendations per deviation
              ReferenceISO 17776 (major accident hazard management in design; HAZID and its checklist); company HSE practiceIEC 61882

              2 · Method

              1. Define scope and basis: V-201 with P-201A/B, the feed control and E-201, C-201 with E-203 and PSV-201, the overhead with E-202, PV-210 and V-202, P-202A/B, the propane rundown and the bottoms to the debutanizer; the SIS, the utilities and the site; the example risk matrix.
              2. Divide the plant into areas on the PFD (section 3).
              3. Apply the guideword checklist to each area (section 4): for every category ask whether the hazard exists here, what could release it (cause / threat) and what would follow (top event and outcome).
              4. Record existing controls, split into prevention (stops the top event) and mitigation (limits the outcome), as in a bow-tie.
              5. Rank the risk (S × L with the controls) and flag major accident hazards (MAH): events that could cause multiple fatalities or major damage, or that escalate beyond the unit (here: into the upstream unit, the debutanizer, the fuel-gas and flare systems).
              6. Assign actions and further studies: design changes, HAZOP nodes, relief and flare review, fire and explosion analysis, SIL assessment, maintenance procedures.

                  Control loop design · depropanizer C-201

                  Teaching slide deck · objectives, degrees of freedom of a distillation column, the LV configuration, why tray 8, pressure by inert venting, loop structures, P/PI/PID and a tuning lab for C-201.
                  Open the deck ↗Same folder (offline / GitHub Pages)

                  Read in order: what must be controlled and why, the vocabulary of a loop, the variables of this unit, its degrees of freedom, the loops on the P&ID, how they were chosen, the loop structures, and finally P, PI and PID with a tuning lab that runs the C-201 model itself. Numbers marked "computed now" are step tests run on a copy of the model when this tab opens; the others come from longer runs on copies of the model made when the tab was written (scripts named in the notes). The running session is never touched.

                  1 Control objectives · 2 The feedback loop · 3 Variables of the unit · 4 Degrees of freedom · 5 Loops on the P&ID · 6 How the loops were chosen · 7 Loop structures · 8 P, PI and PID · 9 Tuning lab

                  1 · Control objectives (ต้องการควบคุมอะไร และเพราะอะไร)

                  Control design starts from objectives, not from instruments. They are ranked: a lower objective is never met by giving up a higher one. On C-201 the first ranks are held by the relief valve, the SIS and the inventory loops; the composition loops look after quality and energy.

                  2 · The feedback loop: parts and vocabulary

                  In this simulator OUT is always shown as % open. FV-204 and PV-210 fail open, so the signal to their actuators is inverted in the field; the operator never sees that inversion. The fail position is chosen for the safe state and is independent of the controller action: PIC-210 is direct acting with a fail-open valve, TIC-208 reverse acting with a fail-closed valve.

                  3 · Variables of the unit classified

                  Every variable is one of: a controlled variable (CV) held at a set point, a manipulated variable (MV) moved by a controller or by the operator, a disturbance (DV) set by the surroundings, a variable that is only indicated or alarmed, or an independent trip measurement read by the SIS.

                  4 · Degrees of freedom (DOF)

                  Why it matters. The degrees of freedom tell the designer how many variables can be held independently. Try to control more CVs than there are independent MVs and controllers fight over one valve; control fewer and some variable drifts wherever the disturbances push it.

                  NDOF = Nvariables − Nindependent equations    and    NDOF = Ndisturbances (fixed by the surroundings) + Nmanipulated

                  For control the useful count is the control DOF = the number of independent manipulated variables: for a process unit, the independent valves (and speeds) that can be set continuously.

                  4.1 DOF of C-201

                  4.2 Check on the model

                  Each of the five steady-state handles is moved on its own on a copy of the model at design (inventory and pressure loops in AUTO, 3 h to steady state). Five independent columns of effect mean five independent handles.

                  4.3 How each DOF is used

                  4.4 DOF of each loop

                  • A feedback loop uses one DOF: it turns "valve position is free" into "CV = SP". The SP becomes the new free input, given by the operator or by a higher controller.
                  • Cascade does not create a DOF. TIC-227 → FIC-204 → FV-204 is still the one valve FV-204: the inner loop fixes the reflux flow, the outer loop chooses which flow. Ratio and feedforward act through the same valve too.
                  • An inventory must use a DOF. A level or a pressure that nothing holds is an integrator: it keeps moving as long as inflow and outflow differ. On C-201 three valves are spent on inventories (sump, reflux drum, vapour); they have no effect on the steady state once the inventory is held, which is why the column has seven valves but five steady-state DOF.
                  • A controller in MAN gives its DOF back to the operator (loop open). A valve at 0 % or 100 % (saturated) loses its DOF: the CV is then uncontrolled. Two controllers must never move one valve at the same time unless a selector or split range decides which one acts.

                  6 · How the loops were chosen for this P&ID (หลักการกำหนด control loop ตาม P&ID)

                    7 · Loop structures: the principle of each (หลักการพื้นฐานของ control loop แต่ละแบบ)

                    8 · Control modes: P, PI and PID (แนวทางการควบคุม P, PI, PID)

                    The simulator's controller (pid() in the model) uses the ideal PID form with every signal in % of the instrument span:

                    OUT(t) = Kc [ e(t) + (1/Ti) ∫e dt − Td dPV/dt ] + bias,   e = SP − PV (reverse action) or PV − SP (direct action)

                    • % of span: PV and SP are converted to % of the range (), so Kc is in % OUT per % PV and does not depend on engineering units. A wide span (TIC-208 0–150 °C) makes 1 °C only 0.67 % of span: the gain must be larger for the same action.
                    • Derivative on PV, not on error, so a set-point change gives no derivative kick; the derivative term is filtered with a time constant Td/8.
                    • Anti-windup: when OUT is clamped at 0 or 100 %, the integral is reset so that OUT sits exactly on the limit; it starts moving back as soon as the error changes sign.
                    • Bumpless transfer and tracking: on any mode change the integral is initialised so OUT does not jump. When FIC-204 is not in CAS, TIC-227 tracks its set point (and rev C LIC-201 tracks FIC-201), ready for a bumpless return to cascade.
                    • Ti = 0 switches the integral off (P only); the bias then keeps the OUT it had, which is why P-only control leaves an offset after a load change.

                    8.1 What each term does

                    ModeActionGoodBadTypical use
                    P (proportional)OUT change ∝ error now.Simple, immediate, stable at low gain.Offset on a self-regulating process: after a load change the error settles at e = Δload / (1 + KcK), not zero. High gain → oscillation.Averaging level control, where offset does not matter.
                    PI (+ integral)Adds the accumulated error; keeps moving OUT until the error is zero.No offset. The industrial default.Slower, more overshoot if Ti is short; windup when the valve saturates (needs anti-windup). On an integrating process (a level) too short a Ti makes the loop oscillate slowly.Every loop on C-201.
                    PID (+ derivative)Adds action ∝ rate of change of PV; anticipates.Faster, less overshoot on slow, lag-dominated loops with a clean signal.Amplifies noise; derivative on error kicks on SP changes (hence derivative on PV).Tray temperatures with several lags in series; rarely on flow or level.

                    8.2 Guidelines by loop type

                    Loop typeModeGainResetDerivativeOn C-201
                    Liquid flowPIlow to moderate (0.1–1)fast, about the valve and line time constant (1–10 s)none (noisy)FIC-201, FIC-204
                    Exchanger outlet temperaturePImoderateabout the exchanger time constant (0.5–2 min)small, optionalTIC-202
                    Tray temperature (composition)PI or PIDdepends strongly on the tray; measure itlong (10–30 min): the column responds slowly and nearly as an integratorhelps when the signal is cleanTIC-208, TIC-227
                    Column pressure by venting inertsPIhigh (little effect per % of vent)long (minutes): the gas inventory changes slowlynonePIC-210
                    Level (averaging)P or PI with long resetlow (≈ 1)long (5–15 min)noneLIC-202, LIC-203, rev C LIC-201: let the level swing so the product flows change smoothly
                    Analyzer (composition)PI, slowlow≥ analyzer dead time + lagnoneAI-219, AI-220 are indicated only; a cascade onto TIC-208 or FIC-204 is a possible upgrade

                    8.3 Tuning from a step test (FOPDT and integrating models)

                    Put the loop in MAN, step OUT, record PV. Self-regulating response (it settles): fit a first-order-plus-dead-time model G(s) = K e−θs/(τs + 1): K = ΔPV/ΔOUT (both in % of span); from the times to 28.3 % and 63.2 % of the final change, τ = 1.5 (t63 − t28), θ = t63 − τ. Lambda (IMC) PI: Kc = τ / [K(λ + θ)], Ti = τ (λ = τ smooth, λ = τ/3 tight).

                    Integrating response (it ramps, like a level): fit G(s) = K′ e−θs/s: K′ = (ramp rate of PV in % per s) / ΔOUT, θ where the tangent at the steepest point meets the starting value. Lambda PI for an integrator: Kc = 1 / [K′(λ + θ)], Ti = 4(λ + θ). A process with a very long time constant (a tray temperature) is treated the same way, from the first part of its response.

                    Dead time limits the gain. In both rules Kc falls as θ rises: a loop that sees a change only after θ seconds cannot react faster than θ, and a high gain on a delayed signal overcorrects and cycles. Anything that adds delay to a loop (slow transmitters, filtering, scan time, sample transport) calls for less gain and a longer reset.

                      HAZOP · Hazard and Operability Study of the depropanizer C-201

                      Teaching slide deck · IEC 61882 phases, the nine nodes of the depropanizer, guide words on a column, a worked worksheet row, relief as the last layer, the dynamic checks on the simulator and the follow-up to LOPA.
                      Open the deck ↗Same folder (offline / GitHub Pages)
                      1 Standard and method · 2 Team and documents · 3 Nodes · 4 Guide words and parameters · 5 Risk matrix · 6 Worksheets · 7 Coverage check · 8 Recommendations · 9 Dynamic check on the simulator · 10 Follow-up and close-out

                      A teaching HAZOP of the depropanizer as drawn on the P&ID tab (rev A), done node by node with the IEC 61882 guide words. Risk ranking uses the example matrix in section 5 (the same one as the HAZID tab); a real study uses the owner's corporate matrix, a multidisciplinary team and the as-built documents.

                      1 · Standard and method (IEC 61882)

                      HAZOP is a structured, team-based examination of a defined system. Each part of the design is compared with its design intent; guide words combined with process parameters generate deviations; for each meaningful deviation the team records causes, consequences, existing safeguards and, where the risk is not acceptable, recommendations. It finds hazards (harm to people, environment, assets) and operability problems (the column cannot make on-spec propane and bottoms, or cannot be run as intended).

                      ReferenceWhat it contributes
                      IEC 61882:2016 Hazard and operability studies (HAZOP studies) – Application guideDefinitions, the four phases (definition, preparation, examination, documentation and follow-up), guide words, team roles, recording
                      CCPS Guidelines for Hazard Evaluation ProceduresWorksheet format, node selection, consequences judged without safeguards, risk ranking, link to LOPA
                      IEC 61511 (functional safety, SIS)How HAZOP scenarios feed LOPA and SIL targets for the trips LSLL-202 and LSHH-203 and for any new high-pressure trip
                      ISO 31000 / owner's risk matrixRisk criteria used to decide whether safeguards are adequate
                      API 520 / API 521 (ISO 23251)Relief scenarios (cooling-water failure, blocked outlet, reflux failure, fire), PSV sizing, flare and depressuring systems
                      API 2510 and NFPA 58 (LPG installations)LPG vessel relief, fire protection, water draining, spacing, BLEVE prevention
                      Thailand: Department of Industrial Works regulation on hazard identification, risk assessment and risk-management plans (B.E. 2543)Legal requirement to identify hazards (HAZOP is an accepted method) and to prepare risk-management plans for factories
                      OSHA 29 CFR 1910.119 (PSM), where applicableA process holding more than about 4.5 t of flammable liquid or gas is covered; this unit holds about t of LPG. Process hazard analysis revalidated at least every five years

                      The four phases

                      1. Definition: scope from the battery limit at the V-201 inlet, through P-201A/B, FV-201, E-201, C-201 with E-203, E-202, V-202, P-202A/B, to the battery limits at the propane rundown (LV-203), the bottoms to the debutanizer (LV-202), the vent to fuel gas (PV-210) and the relief to flare (PSV-201); the SIS (XV-201, XV-202, XV-209) and the utilities as they enter the unit. Excluded: the upstream unit, the debutanizer, the fuel-gas, flare, steam, cooling-water and air systems themselves (their interfaces are recorded as causes and consequences). Objectives, team, risk matrix.
                      2. Preparation: collect the P&ID, PFD, heat and material balance, trip (cause-and-effect) list, alarm list, relief list, procedures and datasheets; divide the unit into nodes; write each node's design intent; choose parameters and guide words.
                      3. Examination: node → design intent → parameter → guide word → is the deviation meaningful? → causes → consequences assuming the safeguards fail → existing safeguards → rank the risk → recommend → next guide word. Every meaningful deviation is recorded, including those with adequate safeguards (full recording), so the reasoning can be audited.
                      4. Documentation and follow-up: worksheets, recommendation register with owners and dates, close-out, revalidation after changes (MOC) or periodically.

                      Consequences are written with no credit for safeguards (worst credible case); the likelihood L is then judged with the listed safeguards working as designed.

                      2 · Team and documents

                      RoleResponsibility
                      HAZOP leader (chair)Independent of the design; runs the method, keeps the team on the node, decides when a deviation is covered
                      Scribe (recorder)Writes the worksheet live, reads back recommendations
                      Process engineer (designer)Design intent, heat and material balance, column hydraulics, relief cases and flare loads
                      Operations representativeHow the column is really run: rounds on LG-201, water draining, pump change-overs, start-up and shutdown, what the operators trust

                      Documents for this study: P&ID tab (rev A with the rev B / rev C upgrades), Process tab (stream table, duties), HAZID tab (PFD DC-PFD-200 and the major hazards), Design and Control loop design tabs (when present), Workbook tab (alarm list and trip settings), and the start-up, shutdown and emergency-shutdown procedures in the Exercises tab.

                      3 · Nodes

                      A node is a section of the plant with one design intent. Boundaries are put where the intent changes: V-201 stores and the pumps raise pressure, FV-201 sets the rate and E-201 vaporizes part of the feed, the stripping and rectifying sections do different separations, the condenser and the vent set the pressure, V-202 holds the condensate that the pumps split into reflux and product, LV-202 sends the bottoms on column pressure alone. Utilities and procedures get their own nodes, because they cause deviations in every other node at once.

                      SSeverity (worst credible consequence)

                      2Medical treatment; off-spec product; small contained release
                      3Lost-time injury; unit shutdown for days; relief to flare; small LPG release
                      4Permanent disability or single fatality; major equipment damage; LPG release with fire

                      Consequences assume the safeguards fail (worst credible case). S ranks that consequence; L ranks its likelihood with the listed safeguards working as designed. Tags marked "recommended addition" are not on the P&ID today. Numbers quoted "in the model" come from runs of the simulator's own model (section 9 and the tab notes).

                      7 · Coverage check: guide words applied in each node

                      A dot means the guide word gave no meaningful deviation for any parameter of the node (it was still considered). EARLY / LATE / BEFORE / AFTER apply mainly to the procedure node N9. The right-hand columns confirm that flow or level, pressure and temperature or heat were examined in the nodes.

                      8 · Recommendation register

                      9 · Dynamic check of selected deviations on the simulator

                      A conventional HAZOP judges consequences qualitatively. Here ten deviations are run on copies of the depropanizer model from the design point with the existing safeguards active (alarms, the SIS trips, the auto-starts, PSV-201, controllers in their normal modes, no operator action) for 30 min, or 60 s past a trip. Alarms are evaluated from the page's alarm list every second with the console's suppression (product and loop alarms only while the column is heated and fed; rev B alarms only with rev B). The runs show whether the safeguards act before harm, and how much time the operator has.

                      Runs when this tab is opened.

                      What the runs tell the HAZOP team

                      • Waiting for the runs…

                      10 · Follow-up and close-out

                      • Each recommendation gets an owner and a due date; the owner answers accepted and done, accepted with an alternative (with justification) or rejected (with justification agreed by the HAZOP leader and the plant manager).
                      • High scenarios whose protection relies on PSV-201, on LSHH-203 or LSLL-202, or on the operator (overpressure from cooling-water loss, a blocked vent or too much reflux; V-201 overfill and fire; LPG leaks) go to LOPA to decide whether a new high-pressure trip is needed and what SIL it must meet (IEC 61511).
                      • The relief recommendations (fire case on V-201 and V-202, simultaneous cooling-water failure on the flare) go to a relief and flare study (API 521).
                      • Any change (rev B LT-201 or rev C LIC-201 in service, a new trip or a changed set point, a different fail position) goes through management of change, which checks whether the HAZOP must be updated.
                      • Interfaces: loss of feed and V-201 overfill to the upstream unit; gas blow-by and off-spec bottoms to the debutanizer HAZOP; vent flow and liquid carry-over to the fuel-gas system owner; simultaneous relief to the flare owner.
                      • Revalidate periodically (typically every five years) and after incidents.
                      • Use the simulator to train operators on the scenarios the HAZOP found, and to check that the procedures and alarm responses really work (section 9).

                      Safety layers · layers of protection for C-201

                      Teaching slide deck · the six protection layers of the depropanizer, the layered P&ID, the trip matrix, integrity operating windows, independence of sensors and the relief, containment and fire rules for an LPG column.
                      Open the deck ↗Same folder (offline / GitHub Pages)
                      1 The six layers · 2 P&ID layer by layer · 3 What each layer does · 4 Integrity operating windows · 5 Independence check · 6 Good practices · 7 Standards

                      Safety must cover failures of equipment (including the control system) and of people, and more than one failure at a time. The response should be limited, keeping production where possible. So protection is built in layers, each independent of the others, with more strength held in reserve as the event gets more serious. The layers are applied here to the depropanizer C-201: a 27-tray column holding about 15 t of liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) at 1.7 MPa g, with feed drum V-201, reflux drum V-202, a steam reboiler and a water-cooled condenser. LPG is flammable, heavier than air when it vaporises, and a vessel it fills can fail violently in a fire (BLEVE). Set points and trip limits are read from the simulator model; values marked "assumed" are for teaching.

                      1 · The six layers

                      LayerJobAutomatic?Needs power / computer?Needs a person?
                      1 BPCSClosed-loop control keeps the column in its operating region (pressure, levels, temperatures, flows)YesYesSupervises
                      2 AlarmsBring an unusual situation to the attention of a personNo actionYesYes: decides
                      3 SISStop part of the process: heat off, and feed off where neededYesYes, but de-energise to tripNo (reset only)
                      4 ReliefPrevent excessive pressure; send the relieved LPG to the flareYes, self-actuatingNoNo
                      5 ContainmentKeep released LPG away from people and ignition; isolate inventories; protect vessels from firePassive or remote-operatedPartlyPartly
                      6 Emergency responseDetect gas and fire, cool vessels, evacuate, fight the fire, give first aidPartly (deluge)PartlyYes

                      Layers 1–4 are the independent protection layers of the automation and the pressure system. Layers 1–3 all need electrical power, computing and communication, so a power or computer failure could take out all three at once. That is why every SIS block valve (XV-201, XV-202, XV-209) closes when its solenoid loses power, and why each control valve has a fail position chosen for safety: steam valves TV-202 and TV-208 fail closed (no heat), the vent PV-210 fails open (the column pressure falls, it cannot rise), reflux FV-204 fails open (the condensate goes back to the column). Relief, containment and emergency response are kept in reserve. Click a ring to open that layer on the P&ID.

                      Start from the bare process (step 0) and add one layer at a time. Each layer draws the instruments and devices it adds in its own colour: green BPCS, gold alarms (the letters of an existing bubble turn gold when an alarm is configured on it, with the limit beside it), orange SIS, red relief, purple containment, blue emergency response. Items drawn dashed are recommended additions (or rev B / rev C upgrades) that are not in service on the rev A plant of P&ID DC3-V1-PID-001.

                      4 · Integrity operating windows

                      Each key variable has a target, alarm limits that still leave time to act, an SIS limit, and a critical limit where damage comes quickly. The arrow is the live value from the simulator (the DCS reading an operator would see). Limits not in the design data are marked "assumed"; limits marked "model" come from runs of the simulator.

                      5 · Independence check

                      Each layer must not share its sensor, logic or final element with the layer below; otherwise one failure can defeat both. An alarm that belongs to an SIS function may share the SIS sensor, because it sits on the SIS system; a trip that shares the control transmitter is a gap. The table was checked against the code of the simulator — which measurement each controller, alarm, trip and auto-start actually reads — not only against the drawing.

API 520 (relief sizing and installation) and API 521 (relief scenarios for columns: cooling-water failure, reflux failure, blocked outlet, abnormal heat input, fire case with the wetted area, gas blow-by through an emptied level-control valve, thermal relief of blocked-in liquid; emergency depressuring; flare and knock-out drum).

                      LOPA · reliability for safety, layers of protection analysis and bow-tie for C-201

                      Teaching slide deck · failure rate and PFD, reliability block diagrams of the C-201 trips, the LOPA equation worked on five depropanizer scenarios, and the bow-tie as many LOPAs at once.
                      Open the deck ↗Same folder (offline / GitHub Pages)
                      A1 Definitions · A2 Failure rate · A3 R(t), PFD, proof testing · A4 Block diagrams · A5 Failure data · B1 LOPA method · B2 Criteria · B3 IPLs · B4 C-201 worksheet · B5 Register · C Bow-tie · Standards

                      The HAZOP tab says what can go wrong; this tab asks how often, and whether the safeguards are reliable enough. Failure data are the course's generic values; SIS trips use SIS-grade (dangerous undetected) rates. Every frequency that is not from the course table is marked "assumed" and is for teaching, not for design. Times and temperatures quoted from "the model" come from runs of the simulator itself.

                      Part A · Reliability for safety

                      A1 · Definitions

                      TermMeaningOn C-201
                      HazardInherent physical or chemical characteristic that can harm people, environment or property (CCPS)About 15 t of LPG (propane and butane) held liquid at up to 1.7 MPa g; the heat input of the reboiler and preheater; a flammable vapour heavier than air
                      Hazardous eventRelease of material or energy that can cause harmColumn overpressure and rupture; gas blow-by into the debutanizer; liquid LPG in the fuel-gas system; an LPG leak that ignites; BLEVE of V-201
                      RiskRisk = consequence × frequencyA fatality (severity 5) that is tolerable only below 10−4 /yr
                      Tolerable / residual riskRisk accepted in context / risk left after protectionThe LOPA target frequency / the mitigated frequency
                      Reliability R(t)Probability of success during an interval of timeLSHH-203 working through a one-year test interval
                      PFDProbability of failure on demand; F(t) = 1 − R(t)The chance that XV-209 does not close when LSLL-202 calls for it
                      Deterministic / probabilistic analysisCan the design keep events within limits / what is the numerical risk and is it tolerablePSV-201 sized for loss of the condenser / LOPA below

                      Is 99.9 % reliability good enough? For a 1-in-1000 failure it would mean an unsafe landing every day at a big airport. Safety needs both plant reliability (business continuity) and safety reliability (hazard prevention and mitigation).

                      A2 · Failure rate from a population

                      λ = ΔNf / (Ns · Δt): failures in the interval divided by the survivors and the interval length. 100 identical units (think of 100 pump mechanical seals) are drawn from a Weibull life model, R(t) = e−(t/α)β; β < 1 is burn-in, β = 1 the useful life (constant λ = 1/α, the exponential model), β > 1 wear-out.



                      A3 · R(t), PFD and proof testing

                      With a constant failure rate R(t) = e−λt and PFD(t) = F(t) = 1 − e−λt ≈ λt when PFD ≪ 0.1. A standby safeguard fails unseen, so its PFD grows until the next proof test restores it: PFDavg = (1/T)∫0Tλt dt = λT/2. MTTF = ∫R dt = 1/λ.

                      SIL 110−2 – 10−110 – 100
                      SIL 210−3 – 10−2100 – 1 000
                      SIL 310−4 – 10−31 000 – 10 000

                      SIF calculator. A safety instrumented function is sensor → logic solver → final element in series; each subsystem can be redundant. The C-201 trips share the SIS logic solver, and both close the single reboiler steam valve XV-209; a two-channel λ is written as "λA / λB". Pick a trip, change the voting, the SIS-grade failure rates or the test interval. Improving reliability: diversity (different technologies), separation (no single point of failure), fail-safe design.

                      SubsystemVotingλ per channel (/yr)PFDavgShare

                      The course method for parallel systems. Three layers against the same hazard, each with an equivalent failure rate (sum of its blocks), combined as parallel systems through MTTF (inclusion–exclusion): 1/λsys = Σ1/λi − Σ1/(λi+λj) + 1/(λ1+λ2+λ3).

                      C-201 sump low-low: BPCS = level sensor LT-202 1.7 + controller 0.2 + control valve LV-202 0.6; alarm = the same LT-202 1.7 + controller 0.2 + operator 1.0; SIS = level switch LS-202 0.015 + logic solver 0.001 + shutdown valve 0.020 + solenoid 0.004. The result is set by the most reliable branch. LOPA (Part B) treats the same layers differently: it multiplies the demand rate by each layer's PFD, and it gives no credit to a layer that shares its sensor with the initiating event — here the alarm and the controller both read LT-202, while LSLL-202 has its own switch.

                      A5 · Failure data used in this tab

                      EquipmentFailure mode / contextGeneric rate (/yr)SIS / safety-grade rate (/yr)

                      Sources used by the course: OREDA and the CCPS Guidelines for Initiating Events and Independent Protection Layers. A generic rate counts all failure modes; an SIS rate counts only dangerous undetected failures of certified equipment. Millions of unit-hours are needed for a confident rate. A generic all-modes rate put into λT/2 is not a PFD: an alarm on a 1.14 /yr flow sensor would come out above 0.5, which is why alarm and BPCS layers take the fixed CCPS credit of 0.1 instead.

                      Part B · Layers of protection analysis (LOPA)

                      B1 · The method

                      1. Take a scenario from the HAZOP (cause → consequence) and rate its severity; the severity sets the target frequency.
                      2. Estimate the initiating event frequency (IEF) from failure data and any enabling condition that must be true at the same time. If several causes lead to the same consequence, work each and add the frequencies.
                      3. Credit each independent protection layer (IPL) with its PFD. A layer that shares a component with the initiating event, or with another credited layer, gets no credit.
                      4. Apply conditional modifiers (occupancy, probability that the event causes harm).
                      5. Compare with the target: RRF = f / target. If RRF > 1, the gap sets the PFD, and so the SIL, of the extra layer.

                      Lecture example: pressure control malfunction 0.1 /yr × high-pressure alarm 0.1 × relief valve 0.01 × occupancy 0.1 = 10−5 /yr against a fatality target of 10−6 /yr → RRF = 10, not acceptable.

                      B2 · Criteria used here (course risk matrix)

                      SeverityTarget risk frequency (/yr)Health and safetyEnvironmentEconomic

                      Likelihood levels by frequency: 5 most likely (~10 /yr), 4 likely (~1), 3 possible (~0.1), 2 rare (~0.01), 1 almost impossible (~0.001); the band boundaries are taken halfway between decades. Risk = severity × likelihood: 1 negligible, 2–6 low, 8–12 medium, 15–20 high, 25 extreme. Target frequencies differ by country (for a fatality about 10−4 to 10−6 /yr). This matrix is stricter than the HAZOP tab's simple ranking bands, which only order the rows.

                      B3 · What counts as an IPL

                      An IPL must be independent of the initiating event and of the other credited layers, specific to the scenario, dependable (its PFD can be justified) and auditable (tested). An alarm needs time: CCPS asks for about 10 minutes between the alarm and the point of no return. Procedures, training, inspection and one-off permissives are safeguards but not IPLs.

                      LayerPFD credited

                      Part C · Bow-tie

                      A bow-tie is several LOPAs drawn around one top event (the moment control of the hazard is lost). Threats on the left pass prevention (control) barriers; consequences on the right sit behind recovery (mitigation) barriers and conditional modifiers. Escalation factors are conditions that defeat a barrier (a bypass, a blocked impulse line). The top-event frequency is the sum of the threat frequencies times their barrier PFDs. Barrier colours follow the Safety layers tab; grey is a procedure or a conditional modifier. Click a barrier to fail it.

                      Transition operation · startup, shutdown, standby, load, feed and campaign changes on C-201

                      Teaching slide deck · the transitions of the depropanizer, startup and shutdown in order with the reasons, the ESD on a cooling-water failure, total-reflux standby, load following, turndown and feed-composition changes, all run on the model.
