                      Follows the course lecture on operating during transitions (Process Operation, with the startup workshop). The Operating windows tab looks at steady states; a transition is the planned transient between an initial and a final condition. Every trend below was produced by running a copy of this simulator's model through the transition with a script (cold startup from the simulator's cold state, shutdown, emergency shutdown, standby and restart, load and feed changes); the live plant is not touched. The graded procedures stay on the Exercises tab.

                      1 Transitions · 2 Before startup · 3 Cold startup · 4 Shutdown and ESD · 5 Standby and restart · 6 Load following · 7 Turndown · 8 Feed and campaign changes · 9 Off-spec storage · 10 What makes transitions hard

                      1 · What a transition is, and which ones C-201 has

                      Transitions are planned transient behaviour between different initial and final conditions. They need their own procedures, strategies, process structure and sometimes extra equipment, because the column was designed for one steady state. C-201 sits between an upstream unit that sends the feed to V-201, propane storage, and the debutanizer that takes the bottoms on pressure; every C-201 transition also moves its neighbours.

                      KindWhen it happensOn C-201Part

                      2 · Before startup: the unit is made ready

                      Done before the procedure starts (lecture list, applied to C-201):

                        Equipment and features that exist mainly for transitions:

                        ItemWhy a transition needs it

                        3 · Startup from cold: the order and the reasons

                        No.StepWhy this order (analysis)Safety concern

                        How fast may the heat come in, and when should propane be drawn? The same script as the page's expert reference (graded 10/10) was run from the cold state with one thing changed at a time. Times are from the start of the feed pump; "lined out" is the graded condition: 10 minutes at 60 m³/h with both products on spec and the pressure at 1.70 ± 0.03 MPa g.

                        Events in the selected run

                        4 · Shutdown and emergency shutdown: heat off first, the heat sink last

                        No.StepWhy this order (analysis)Safety concern

                        Emergency shutdown on a cooling-water failure: every minute of heat goes to the flare

                        With no cooling water, E-202 condenses nothing: all the boil-up stays as vapour and the pressure rises to the PSV-201 set point (). The graded ESD procedure stops the heat first. The run below loses the cooling water at 20 s (FI-216 falls to zero in 20 s) and applies the ESD after different delays, then closes the draws, stops the reflux pumps and holds the pressure with PV-210 closed, as the procedure says.

                        5 · Standby on total reflux, and the restart after a trip

                        When the feed must stop for a while (the upstream unit is down, the debutanizer cannot take bottoms, storage is full) the column does not have to be shut down: it can be held on total reflux, with the feed and both draws stopped and all the condensate returned. It keeps its pressure, its heat and much of its composition profile, so it is back on spec much sooner than after a cold start. Two ways of holding the heat were run for 60 minutes, then the feed was restored in the same steps as the startup:

                        6 · Load following: the upstream unit raises its rate

                        C-201 takes what the upstream unit sends; V-201 is a small surge drum, not storage (the Process reliability tab gives its hold-up in minutes). When the upstream unit raises its rate, FIC-201 is raised with it and the upstream supply follows the same set point in these runs, so V-201 stays level. Feed 60 → 66 and 60 → 70 m³/h at several ramp rates, with every other loop as at design (TIC-208 on tray 8, reflux FIC-204 fixed at 49 m³/h, the TIC-227 cascade off):

                        7 · Turndown: how low can the feed go?

                        A column turned down keeps its trays but loses vapour: below about 30 % of the flood vapour rate the liquid weeps through the holes and the trays lose efficiency. The pressure control is also sized for design: PV-210 vents less gas at low load and runs out of controllable opening. Steady states from the model with the reflux left at design or reduced in proportion to the feed (TIC-208 on tray 8):

                        8 · Feed-composition and campaign changes

                        The upstream unit may change its operation or feed slate: the feed becomes lighter (more propane) or heavier (more butane and heavier). A campaign is a planned block of operation with different targets (for example a tighter propane specification). Each change is a transition between two steady states, and the product made on the way may be off spec. The feed composition was changed at 1 min (light key z from , reaching the new value with a 1-min lag) with the reflux fixed (as at design) and with the top-temperature cascade TIC-227 → FIC-204 in service:

                        9 · How big must the off-spec tank be?

                        Off-spec product made during a transition is not lost: it goes to an off-spec (slop) tank and is fed back slowly to V-201 with the fresh feed, or sold at the lower price. The tank must hold the off-spec made in one transition plus what is still waiting from the last one; the model runs above give the volume per event. V = Σ (events × off-spec per event) over the rework period, and the rework takes V / (rework rate) hours.

                        10 · Batch processes, and what makes column transitions hard

                        Batch distillation (all the charge at the start, the cuts taken one after the other) never reaches a steady state: every batch is a transition. C-201 is continuous, so its transitions are the ones above.

                          References: course lecture on operating during transitions and the process startup workshop (Process Operation); T. Marlin, Process Operability class materials; general distillation practice (total-reflux startup, venting of non-condensables, flooding and weeping limits, turndown).

                          1 Definitions · 2 Failure rate and life · 3 Structures · 4 The standby lesson · 5 C-201 as a series system · 6 Design for reliability · 7 Fouling and the cleaning interval · 8 Inventory · 9 Maintenance · 10 Life-cycle cost

                          1 · Reliability, availability and why they differ

                          TermDefinitionOn C-201

                          Availability is not reliability. A column that trips twelve times a year but restarts in an hour each time has high availability and poor reliability: every trip is a restart on total reflux, off-spec bottoms to the debutanizer and a message to the upstream unit to stop sending. The course example: three years of the same plant with uptimes 6815, 7612 and 8471 h of 8760 h.

                          2 · Failure rate, the bathtub and the exponential model

                          Failure rate λ(t) = failures per unit time divided by the items still working. Over life it often follows the bathtub: infant mortality (falling λ), chance failures (constant λ), wear-out (rising λ). Most real equipment does not follow the full bathtub (reliability-centred maintenance studies found six patterns, most without wear-out), so the right maintenance depends on the pattern. With constant λ:

                          R(t) = e−λt,   F(t) = 1 − R(t),   MTTF = 1/λ

                          At t = MTTF only 37 % survive (63.2 % have failed). Course example: λ = 0.0001 /h → MTTF 10 000 h; R(5000 h) = e−0.5 = 0.61. The Weibull model R(t) = exp[−(t/η)β] covers all three regions with the shape β:

                          3 · Structures: series, parallel, standby, k out of N

                          A plant is many components joined in structures; the structure sets the system reliability. All formulas assume independent failures (no common cause) and, for standby, perfect switching.

                          StructureWorks whenReliabilityMTTF (identical elements, λ each)C-201 example

                          4 · The standby lesson: a spare is only as good as the time it takes to start

                          C-201 has two spared services: the feed pumps (P-201A motor, P-201B steam turbine, auto-start on FSLL-201) and the reflux pumps (P-202A/B, auto-start on PDSL-230). The formulas of part 3 assume the standby takes over at once. How long can the column wait? The running pump was stopped on a copy of the model at design and the spare started automatically, by hand after a delay, or not at all (every other loop as at design, 60 min):

                          5 · C-201 as a series system: what stops the on-spec product, and how often

                          For production every element in the chain feed pump → feed valve and preheat → column trays → reboiler and LP steam → condenser and cooling water → reflux pump → pressure and product control → analyzers → trips must work, so C-201 is a series system: λsys = Σ λi × fi, where fi is the fraction of element i's failures that stop the on-spec product (a trip, lost feed or reflux, a forced cleaning). Each outage costs the repair or switching time plus the restart measured on the model (Transition operation tab): . Toggle design changes and watch outages, availability and the Pareto.

                          6 · Design for reliability

                          Lecture principleWhat it meansC-201 as builtGap or recommendation

                          7 · Operating for reliability: fouling and the cleaning interval

                          The lecture's trade-off: a short-term gain (running on, pushing a variable toward a constraint) against long-term life. On C-201 the slow killers are fouling of the reboiler E-203 (TIC-208 has to open TV-208 further for the same boil-up) and fouling of the condenser E-202 (less surface, so the pressure controller has to work its vent valve harder and PV-210 opens further). The model was run to steady state (owRun, loops as at design) at increasing fouling severity; pick a case, set a fouling rate, and read when the valve margin is gone:

                          10 · Life-cycle cost: how many reflux pumps?

                          Life-cycle costing adds to the usual profitability analysis the costs that reliability changes: maintenance and spares, failure frequency, the cost of each failure (repair, lost and off-spec production, restart) and the extra equipment for redundancy. The course example asks how many pumps to install. The outage cost starts from the model's design margin and the restart time from the Transition operation tab; pump prices are assumed teaching values.

                          Economic basis

                          1 · Efficiency, optimisation and their place among the priorities

                          Efficiency (in operation, the same as optimisation) is good economic performance: the products delivered at the rate and quality needed with less energy, raw material and effluent, and less environmental impact. For energy: efficiency = useful output ÷ energy input; for a column the useful output is a separation, so the practical measures are the steam per unit of product and the margin per hour.

                          Four ways to improve it: design with the right capacities (trays, reboiler, condenser); use the existing equipment in the most efficient way (no over-purification, no needless venting); choose a better process structure (heat integration, pressure); choose the best operating conditions inside the window (parts 5–8).

                          Efficiency is not first. On C-201 the product specs and the throughput are worth far more than the steam (part 4): an operator never trades a higher priority for energy.

                          PriorityObjectiveOn C-201

                          2 · The energy picture now

                          Live from the running simulator, next to the design state. The heat enters as LP steam in two places (E-201 preheats and partly vaporizes the feed, E-203 boils up from the sump) and leaves almost entirely to the cooling water in E-202; the separation itself consumes little: it only moves the heat from about 110 °C to about 45 °C.

                          3 · Where the energy goes

                          Energy balance of the unit, feed at its supply temperature as the reference (live). In: the heat of the two steams. Out: the condenser duty to the cooling water, the sensible heat the products carry away (the bottoms leave hot to the debutanizer, the propane leaves subcooled), the vent gas. The model uses constant molar overflow with one latent heat, so its enthalpy balance does not close exactly: the remainder is shown, not hidden.

                          4 · Economics: what the column earns, and what matters most

                          The operating margin from the page's own economics (econ()): products at their on-spec or off-spec price, less feed, steam, cooling water and flare, plus the vent gas credited as fuel gas. Live and at design:

                          5 · Over-purification: reflux, boil-up and product purity

                          A purer product than the spec asks for costs reflux, and reflux has to be boiled up again. The left chart moves the reflux at the design tray-8 set point (Type I runs); the right chart holds one product at its design purity and moves the target of the other (the page found the reflux and tray-8 set points of each point on the model).

                          6 · Column pressure and energy

                          Lower pressure raises the relative volatility of propane over butane (the vapour pressures diverge as the temperature falls), so fewer stages' worth of reflux and boil-up give the same split. But the overhead must still condense against the cooling water: the lower the pressure, the lower the condensing temperature and the less the condenser can do, until the gas pocket is fully vented and PV-210 runs out. Each point below holds both purities at their design values. Two ways to compare: with the feed entering in the same state (its vapour fraction held, so TIC-202 moves with the pressure), or with TIC-202 left at its set point, as an operator who only moves PIC-210 would do.

                          7 · Feed preheat against reboiler steam

                          Heat put into the feed by E-201 enters at the feed tray, not at the bottom: it makes vapour that only the rectifying section sees. Both exchangers burn the same LP steam, so the question is whether a tonne in the preheater saves a tonne in the reboiler. Each point holds both purities at design.

                          8 · Best operating conditions: push toward the spec

                          The cheapest purity is the one at the spec, but an analyzer reading scatters around its mean, and every excursion above the spec sells product at the off-spec price. The best target sits below the spec by a margin set by the variability. The page combines the steam and yield effect of the target (part 5, model) with the probability of an excursion (normal distribution of AI-219 around its target, assumed) and the off-spec price.

                          Industrial practice: reduce the variability first (better control, a faster analyzer, a composition loop on the top), then move the target toward the spec; move slowly and from a model where one exists; change targets and alarm limits through management of change, never by habit.

                          9 · Propane lost with the vent gas

                          The non-condensables leave through PV-210 to fuel gas saturated with propane: the vent gas is only as rich in inerts as the gas pocket in E-202 allows (in the model the vent carries 25 % inerts when the pocket is gone, more as the pocket grows). Every Nm³ of propane vented is sold as fuel gas instead of as propane. Model runs at design feed:

                          1 What an SOP is · 2 Format · 3 SOP register · 4 SOP viewer · 5 Writing rules · 6 Life of an SOP

                          1 · What an SOP is, and which activities need one

                          A standard operating procedure is the written, approved way to carry out one task: the same steps, in the same order, with the same checks, whoever is on shift. It turns the reasons worked out on the other tabs (startup order, operating window, trips, spare pumps) into actions an operator can follow under pressure.

                          Process safety management requires written procedures for each operating phase (OSHA 29 CFR 1910.119(f)): initial startup, normal operations, temporary operations, emergency shutdown (including who decides and when), emergency operations, normal shutdown, and startup after a turnaround or an emergency shutdown; plus the operating limits with the consequences of deviation and the steps to correct or avoid it, the safety and health considerations (hazards, precautions, exposure control), and the safety systems and their functions. Procedures must be readily available, certified as current each year, and cover safe work practices such as lockout/tagout, line opening and sampling.

                          6 · The life of an SOP

                          Draft from the design intent and the hazard studies (HAZID, HAZOP, LOPA) → verify on the simulator (the graded procedures in the Exercises tab check the same steps) → review by operations, process and safety → approve and train → use, with every deviation reported → review after any change (management of change), after an incident or near miss, and at the fixed interval (certified annually under PSM), then revise and re-issue.

                          References: OSHA 29 CFR 1910.119(f) Operating procedures and (j) mechanical integrity; OSHA 29 CFR 1910.147 Control of hazardous energy (lockout/tagout); CCPS, Guidelines for Writing Effective Operating and Maintenance Procedures; general LPG practice for sampling and line opening; Thai Department of Industrial Works notification on process safety management.
